passage:
At Diwali, Chaitanya Uncle held up Siddharth's report card for the whole room. "Full marks in maths! This boy will go far." Nirmala, ten, stood by the sweets tray and felt her chest pinch. Nobody had asked about her drawing prize. She decided she must be the less loved one, and the comparison stuck to her like a burr.

After that she counted everything. Siddharth got the bigger laddoo. He stayed up until nine. He got the tablet for an hour on Sunday. "Same for me," she told Amma, every time, holding up fingers. "Exactly the same." When Amma gave her a hug and no argument, it did not seem to count.

On Tuesday Siddharth failed a spelling test. Nirmala chanted, "Full marks in maths, zero in spelling!" in the hallway, then ran to the kitchen, hoping for Amma's approval. "Amma, he hid his paper under the sofa!" she announced, standing very straight.

Amma, tired and stirring dal after a long shift, sighed without turning round. "Nirmala, please." Siddharth stood in the doorway, jaw set, and later that night he slammed his door. He had not hidden anything. Nirmala stayed on the stairs, unsure why the smile she had expected never came.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya Uncle hold up at Diwali?
qa.a: He held up Siddharth's report card in front of everyone.

qa.q: How did the praise at Diwali connect to Nirmala's counting and her tattling on Tuesday?
qa.a: The comparison made her feel less loved, so she counted shares and demanded the same for herself, then chanted at Siddharth's failure and ran to tell on him for Amma's approval, leaving him angry and Amma tired.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling at the sweets tray when Uncle praised Siddharth?
qa.a: She felt hurt and overlooked, believing she was the less loved one because nobody asked about her drawing prize.

qa.q: What could Amma do to reach the need beneath Nirmala's counting?
qa.a: She could spend a little time on Nirmala's drawing prize and praise her own effort, so she does not need equal shares to know she matters.

grounding: Three early stages of a sibling rivalry cycle: comparison after a relative's praise, counting who gets more, and teasing and tattling that leave both children worse off.

passage:
Meher, seven, stood at the edge of the veranda while Santosh and Tarun built a fort out of cushions. "You can be the guard," Santosh said, pointing to the doorstep, "because you're small." She stamped her foot. "That's not fair! I'm the one who found the blanket!" What she wanted was to be the captain, at least once, and not merely be tolerated.

Papa Hrithik had stopped saying "why can't you be like your brother" months ago. Now he said, "Santosh, that drawing has a lot of patience in it," and "Tarun, thanks for fixing the wheel." When the boys quarrelled over the last mango, he stood at the door and waited. "What could work for both of you?" They split it, grumbling, and he went back to his newspaper.

That Saturday Dada sat on the park bench with his tea. A big boy had knocked Meher's ball into the drain and laughed. Before Dada could rise, Santosh and Tarun were both there. "That's her ball," Santosh said. "Get it out," said Tarun. The big boy backed away.

Walking home, the three of them were arguing again about whose turn it was to hold the ball. Dada smiled into his cup.

qa.q: What was Meher's role in the cushion fort before she protested?
qa.a: Santosh assigned her to be the guard at the doorstep because she was small.

qa.q: How did the way Papa Hrithik handled the children differ from before, and how did it show up at the park?
qa.a: He stopped comparing them, praised each child for their own effort, and let them solve small quarrels, and at the park the same brothers who quarrel defended Meher against a bigger boy.

qa.q: What was Meher feeling when she stamped her foot on the veranda?
qa.a: She felt left out and bossed around, and wanted to be taken seriously as captain instead of just tolerated.

qa.q: What might Dada's smile suggest about how he sees the siblings?
qa.a: He sees that the rivalry and loyalty live together, and that their fights do not mean they lack a bond that will last.

grounding: Three later stages of a sibling rivalry cycle: the younger child feeling bossed, a parent who stops comparing, and a grandparent seeing the siblings defend each other.

passage:
Yash was nineteen the night he finally asked it, in the small study circle after Sunday prayers: "What if I can't believe some of this?" A few people shifted in their seats. Shalini put down her cup and smiled. "That question is older than any of us in this room," she said. "Sit with it, and come back and tell me what you find." Nobody scolded him, and he left feeling curious more than afraid.

By the second year at college he had stopped going to the prayers in the hostel. He borrowed books from the library that he would have hidden from his grandmother, argued late into the night with Tenzin, who practised another faith, and with Rohan, who practised none. The old certainty loosened like a jar lid. It felt like freedom, and also like losing a room in the house he had grown up in.

In March he woke on a Sunday and felt nothing. No anger, no relief, just a quiet where the meaning had sat. He walked to the tea stall, sat with his cup, and did not pretend to have an answer. He wrote one line to Shalini: "Still asking." She answered the same evening: "Good. Keep asking honestly."

qa.q: Where did Yash first ask his question about belief?
qa.a: He asked in the small study circle after Sunday prayers.

qa.q: How did Shalini's answer differ from what Yash might have feared, and how did it matter later in March?
qa.a: She met his question with interest, said it was very old and common, and did not shame him, so when he felt empty in March he could still write to her honestly and get a welcome.

qa.q: What was Yash feeling when he woke up on the Sunday in March?
qa.a: He felt hollow and quiet, with no anger or relief, and did not pretend to have an answer.

qa.q: How could Yash respond to the emptiness without rushing to a firm conclusion?
qa.a: He can keep asking honestly and stay in touch with people who welcome his questions, such as Shalini, instead of forcing an answer.

grounding: Three stages of a faith journey through doubt: an elder welcoming first questions, distance and loosened certainty away from home, and a quiet emptiness that is allowed to stay unresolved.

passage:
At the Friday dinner, Hemant said, "Sangeeta's storyboards are honestly amazing. She has such an eye." Sunaina nodded and reached for the rice, but something small shrank inside her. She had never heard him say that about her sketches. She started sizing herself up beside a woman she had met once, and always came out short.

Over the next fortnight the shrinking got more inventive. His reply came four hours late and she decided it meant something. He liked a group photo and she zoomed in to find who stood beside him. He went out for a colleague's leaving drinks, and she lay awake.

Then she began to test him. "Maybe you'd rather be with someone more artistic," she said with a laugh that was not quite a laugh. She stopped answering his texts for a day to see whether he would come knocking at her door. When he left the room for a call, she opened his phone and scrolled, heart in her throat, and found nothing except a pizza order and a photo of his cat.

Hemant came back in and stood still, his face changing. "What were you looking for?" he asked. Sunaina put the phone down and did not know what to say.

qa.q: What did Hemant say about Sangeeta at the Friday dinner?
qa.a: He said her storyboards were honestly amazing and that she has an eye for them.

qa.q: How did the praise for Sangeeta at dinner lead to Sunaina's later testing, and did the tests reassure her?
qa.a: The praise made her compare herself and feel small, then she read ordinary events like a slow reply as evidence and started testing Hemant with jokes, silence and checking his phone, but the tests found nothing and left both of them worn down.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling as she scrolled through Hemant's phone?
qa.a: She felt anxious and insecure, with her heart in her throat, and was afraid of what she might find.

qa.q: What could Sunaina say to Hemant instead of testing him?
qa.a: She could tell him honestly that the praise made her feel small and that she wants to work on her own confidence, without demanding proof.

grounding: Three early stages of a jealousy spiral in a young couple: comparison with a praised colleague, reading neutral events as evidence, and testing and checking the partner.

passage:
Manav had started closing his laptop when Jaya walked past. He was not hiding anything, but her sharp questions about who he messaged made him feel like a suspect, and he wanted a place where nobody watched him. Jaya noticed the closed lid and her stomach turned: he was hiding something. His privacy and her suspicion fed each other week after week.

After a bad evening she called Seema, who listened until she had finished. "This isn't really about Manav, is it?" said Seema. "It's about how you see yourself when you compare." Jaya was silent, then quietly said, "I feel like I'm not enough."

The next day she sat opposite Manav on the balcony. "When you go quiet after work I feel insecure, and that's mine to work on," she said. "I'd like a little reassurance, but I won't ask you to prove anything." Manav's shoulders came down. "Thanks for telling me," he said, "I'll try to be easy to reach."

That month Jaya rejoined the climbing wall and booked three sessions with Nandini, the college counsellor. Manav left his phone on the table and answered plainly. On days the old fear came back, Jaya breathed slowly, called Seema, and let it pass. Trust grew slowly, from both sides.

qa.q: Who did Jaya call after the bad evening?
qa.a: She called Seema.

qa.q: How did Jaya's suspicion and Manav's privacy affect each other, and what changed after Jaya spoke on the balcony?
qa.a: His closed laptop and her questions fed each other, each confirming the other's story, but when Jaya owned her insecurity without accusing him, Manav relaxed and promised to be easy to reach.

qa.q: What was Manav feeling when Jaya kept asking who he messaged?
qa.a: He felt distrusted and watched, like a suspect, so he sought private space.

qa.q: What did Jaya do to build her own security?
qa.a: She rejoined the climbing wall, saw the counsellor Nandini, and called Seema when the fear came back, which worked on her own worth instead of relying on checking.

grounding: Three later stages of a jealousy spiral: mutual defensiveness feeding itself, owning the feeling without accusing, and building inner security alongside the partner's openness.

passage:
The teacher put Rajni next to Varun, and for the first week they said nothing to each other. Then Varun's pencil case fell open and a stack of cricket cards slid across the floor. Rajni gasped. "You have the Mumbai captain!" she whispered. By break they were trading behind the water cooler, and by Friday the bench felt like theirs.

On Monday Rajni gave Varun half her tiffin's puri and told him, very quietly, that she was scared of the dark. She watched his face. If he laughed, that would be the end. Varun only nodded. "I hate lifts," he said. Every day they offered each other something a bit bigger and each time checked what happened next.

Soon they walked home together, invented a code of knocks on the desk, and Rajni announced, "You are my best friend." Varun grinned so wide his ears moved.

At the next recess Aditi asked Rajni to skip rope. Rajni went, laughing. Varun stood by the wall with his cards, chewing his lip. When Rajni came back he said, "I'm not trading with you anymore," and turned his back. Rajni stared at his shoulders, confused and a little cross.

qa.q: What did Varun's cards do that first made Rajni speak to him?
qa.a: They slid out of his pencil case onto the floor, and Rajni noticed the Mumbai captain.

qa.q: How did the first week differ from the days that followed, and what test did Rajni give the friendship along the way?
qa.a: At first they sat together silently, but shared cards and a bench started the friendship, and then Rajni shared puri and her fear of the dark while watching Varun's face to see whether he would laugh.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling as he stood by the wall while Rajni skipped rope?
qa.a: He felt hurt and left out, and possessive of his best friend, which is why he turned his back and refused to trade.

qa.q: What could Rajni do to repair the moment with Varun?
qa.a: She could tell him she still counts him as her best friend and suggest a plan for them both, such as trading cards after school.

grounding: Three early stages of a friendship forming between children: shared interest and proximity, testing trust with small disclosures, and becoming best friends with the first hurt of possessiveness.
